world.bio: I tuned and repaired pianos across Toronto for 45 years, from concert halls to church basements to living rooms in Scarborough. Retired four years now. Since then I have collected unwanted uprights and restored them in my garage in Etobicoke. Has four restored, playable uprights in the garage that I want to give to community groups; the rest are still waiting for felts, strings or patience.
skills_assets: Forty-five years of tuning, regulation and restoration on uprights and grands
A garage workshop with a bench, a stringing frame and a cabinet of old hammers and felts
A trailer hitch and a borrowed piano dolly with straps
A network of former customers, church musicians and music teachers
A habit of keeping every dead key, in case it is needed
A reliable friend, Dmitri, who helps lift when the pianos go in or out

projects.name: The garage pianos
projects.text: Six donated upright pianos in the garage, restored since retirement; four are playable now. The other two need new bass strings and a full re-felt. I log each one in a notebook: make, serial number, where it came from, what has been done. Two Mason & Risch, one Heintzman, one Willis, a Gerhard Heintzman and an unnamed Canadian-built spinet I am fond of. Every winter I tell myself I will finish them all. Every spring, there is another one on the kerb.

projects.name: Sourdough
projects.text: Third loaf was a brick. Fourth was a very good brick. Helen says it is the flour; I say it is the oven; we both know it is me.

projects.name: Maple Leafs season tickets chat group
projects.text: A group of five old men who watch the games on the phone and complain by text. The team is the same as ever. Hope fades; the group does not.

notes.text: Finished the third action on the Heintzman. The keys are even now. Played a scale and felt the old thing push back. A piano is one of the few objects that answers you.
Helen had her knee operation three weeks ago and is walking with the physio. She has no patience for the exercises. I carry her tea and say nothing. That is, I say it is a very nice knee.
Counted: six uprights, one spinet frame, a pile of keys. Four play. Two need strings. The garage smells of felt and old wood and I love it and I understand it is a problem.
Maple Leafs lost to a team I did not know existed. Group chat is silent. Even the optimists have gone to bed.
Sourdough starter smells like pears now. Helen sniffed and said "that cannot be good". I said it is very good. She said it is a bin.

Helen and I argued about the garage again. She says the garage must be cleared before the first snow or she will call the junk removal company herself. I said the pianos are not junk. She said "Walter, there are six of them and we have one car". Which is a fair point. We did not speak at dinner. I went out and sat in the car in the driveway, looking at the garage door. She came out at nine with tea and said nothing. We are both stubborn.
Called Dmitri to ask if he knows anyone with a van. He asked how many pianos. I said four that are ready. He said "who is getting them?" I said I have not decided. He said "that is the problem".
Walked past a church whose piano I tuned for twenty years. A young man was carrying it out the side door onto a skip. It was a good Mason & Risch. I almost stopped him. I did not.
Gave the notebook another read. Four of these are good enough that I would put my name on them. I want them to go to people who will play them badly and often.
First frost warning for the weekend. The weather channel says snow by early November. I have six weeks, and I have not told Helen I know the date.

messages.text: Helen: Walter, the physio says I should walk more. Me: I will walk with you. Helen: Not to the garage. Me: Not to the garage.
Dmitri: I can borrow a truck on Saturday week. Me: How much will it cost? Dmitri: A coffee. Me: A big one.
Karen: Dad, how is the garage? Me: Full. Karen: Mum says she will call a company. Me: She says that every year. Karen: This year she means it.

Mrs. Eng: Do you still have a small upright? My granddaughter wants to learn. Me: I have a few. I am still deciding where they go. Mrs. Eng: I can pay. Me: I do not want to sell them, I want them used.
Gord: They lost again. Me: I know. Gord: Hope? Me: None. Gord: Same time Saturday.

calendar.event: Finish stringing the Willis, all day
Sourdough lesson at the library, 2 p.m.

relations.about: Wife of forty-eight years, recovering from knee surgery
Old friend who helps with the heavy lifting

constraints: Does not sell; wants the pianos to be played
Cannot lift heavy items alone any more
Garage has to be cleared before snow
Will not give a piano to anyone who plans to resell it
sensitive: Argument with his wife over the garage is getting worse
His hands shake a little now; fine work gets harder
He fears that if the pianos go, he has nothing to do
